# 1 Kings Chapter 11 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A)

---

**1** King Solomon loved many foreign women besides Pharaoh's daughter — women from Moab, Ammon, Edom, Sidon, and the Hittites.

**2** They came from the very nations about which the LORD had told the Israelites, "You must not intermarry with them, because they will surely turn your hearts to their gods." Yet Solomon held fast to them in love.

**3** He had seven hundred wives of royal birth and three hundred concubines — and his wives led his heart astray.

**4** As Solomon grew old, his wives turned his heart toward other gods. His heart was no longer fully devoted to the LORD his God, as his father David's heart had been.

**5** Solomon followed Ashtoreth the goddess of the Sidonians and Milcom the detestable god of the Ammonites.

**6** Solomon did what was evil in the LORD's sight. He did not follow the LORD completely, as his father David had done.

**7** On the hill east of Jerusalem, Solomon built a shrine for Chemosh, the detestable god of Moab, and for Molech, the detestable god of the Ammonites.

**8** He did the same for all his foreign wives, who burned incense and offered sacrifices to their gods.

**9** The LORD became angry with Solomon because his heart had turned away from the LORD, the God of Israel, who had appeared to him twice

**10** and had specifically warned him about this very thing — not to follow other gods. But Solomon refused to obey.

**11** So the LORD said to Solomon, "Since you have done this and have not kept my covenant and my decrees, which I commanded you, I will certainly tear the kingdom away from you and give it to one of your subordinates.

**12** But for the sake of your father David, I will not do it during your lifetime. I will tear it out of your son's hand.

**13** Yet I will not tear away the entire kingdom. I will leave your son one tribe, for the sake of my servant David and for the sake of Jerusalem, which I have chosen."

**14** Then the LORD raised up an adversary against Solomon — Hadad the Edomite, from the royal family of Edom.

**15** Years earlier, when David was fighting in Edom and Joab the army commander had gone to bury the dead, Joab had struck down every male in Edom.

**16** Joab and all the Israelites stayed there six months, until they had killed every male.

**17** But Hadad, still a young boy, escaped to Egypt with some of his father's Edomite officials.

**18** They left Midian, traveled through Paran, picked up more men along the way, and arrived in Egypt. Pharaoh gave Hadad a house, a food allowance, and land.

**19** Hadad gained such favor with Pharaoh that the king gave him his wife's sister — Queen Tahpenes's sister — in marriage.

**20** Tahpenes's sister bore him a son, Genubath, whom Tahpenes raised in the palace alongside Pharaoh's own children.

**21** When Hadad heard in Egypt that David had died and that Joab the army commander was also dead, he said to Pharaoh, "Let me go home to my own country."

**22** "What have you lacked here that makes you want to leave?" Pharaoh asked. "Nothing," Hadad replied, "but please let me go."

**23** God also raised up another adversary against Solomon — Rezon son of Eliada, who had deserted his master, King Hadadezer of Zobah.

**24** After David's victories, Rezon gathered a band of rebels and went to Damascus, where they settled and he became king.

**25** Rezon was hostile to Israel throughout Solomon's reign, compounding the trouble caused by Hadad. He ruled over Aram and was a constant threat to Israel.

**26** There was also Jeroboam son of Nebat, an Ephraimite from Zeredah. His mother Zeruah was a widow. He was one of Solomon's officials, and he rebelled against the king.

**27** This is the story of his rebellion: Solomon was building the Millo, closing the gap in the wall of the City of David.

**28** Jeroboam was an exceptionally capable man. When Solomon noticed how industrious this young man was, he put him in charge of the entire labor force of the tribes of Joseph.

**29** One day, as Jeroboam was leaving Jerusalem, the prophet Ahijah of Shiloh met him on the road. Ahijah was wearing a new cloak, and the two of them were alone in the countryside.

**30** Ahijah grabbed the new cloak he was wearing and ripped it into twelve pieces.

**31** He said to Jeroboam, "Take ten pieces for yourself, because this is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: 'I am about to tear the kingdom out of Solomon's hand and give you ten tribes.

**32** He will keep one tribe, for the sake of my servant David and for the sake of Jerusalem, the city I chose from all the tribes of Israel.

**33** I am doing this because they have abandoned me and worshiped Ashtoreth goddess of Sidon, Chemosh god of Moab, and Milcom god of Ammon. They have not walked in my ways or done what is right in my eyes or kept my laws and regulations as David, Solomon's father, did.

**34** But I will not take the whole kingdom from Solomon. I will let him be ruler for the rest of his life, for the sake of my servant David, whom I chose because he obeyed my commands and decrees.

**35** I will take the kingdom from his son and give you ten tribes.

**36** I will give his son one tribe so that my servant David will always have a lamp burning before me in Jerusalem, the city I chose as the place for my name.

**37** As for you, I will take you, and you will rule over everything your heart desires. You will be king over Israel.

**38** If you obey everything I command you, walk in my ways, and do what is right in my eyes by keeping my decrees and commands as my servant David did, I will be with you. I will build you a dynasty as enduring as the one I built for David, and I will give you Israel.

**39** I will humble David's descendants because of this — but not forever.'"

**40** Solomon tried to kill Jeroboam, but Jeroboam fled to Egypt, to King Shishak, and stayed there until Solomon died.

**41** As for the rest of Solomon's reign — everything he did and the wisdom he showed — it is all recorded in the Book of the Acts of Solomon.

**42** Solomon reigned in Jerusalem over all Israel for forty years.

**43** Then Solomon died and was buried in the City of David. His son Rehoboam succeeded him as king.

---
## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

1. **11:1-3 — the three violations complete**: Deuteronomy 17 forbids Israel's king from accumulating horses (ch. 10), wealth (ch. 10), and wives (ch. 11). Solomon has now violated all three — systematically, extravagantly, and without apparent remorse. The wisest man in history fails the simplest test.

2. **11:4 — "no longer fully devoted"**: The Hebrew says his heart was "not shalem" — not complete, not whole. Solomon's name (Shelomoh) means "his peace" or "his wholeness." The narrator is saying: Solomon is no longer Solomon. He has become the opposite of his own name.

3. **11:7 — shrines on the hill**: Solomon builds pagan altars on the Mount of Olives — within direct line of sight of the temple. The architectural insult is deliberate: the man who built God's house now builds houses for God's rivals, and puts them where the temple can see them.

4. **11:29-31 — the torn cloak**: Ahijah's prophetic theater mirrors the moment when Samuel's robe tore before Saul (1 Sam 15:27-28). Same action, same meaning: the kingdom is being ripped away. The united monarchy ends the same way it lost its first king.

5. **11:36 — "a lamp"**: God preserves one tribe for David's line so that David's lamp will never go out. This is the most fragile form of hope — a single candle in a dynasty of darkness. But it is enough. The lamp of David will burn until a greater son sits on his throne.

— PNEUMA
